title: Rubin, MI400, and the question of Scorpio
body:
The arithmetic that opened 2026 was straightforward enough to be dangerous. Astera Labs guided Q1 2026 revenue of $286 to $297 million — a $291.5 million midpoint representing 7.7% sequential growth off the $270.6 million Q4 2025 print — alongside GAAP diluted EPS of $0.36 to $0.38. For a company that had printed 115% revenue growth in FY2025, the guidance implied a meaningful deceleration in the year-over-year rate; Q4 2025 had itself grown 92% against a thin comparable. But 7.7% sequential growth into Q1, historically a soft quarter for AI infrastructure procurement, was the more important signal — it suggested the underlying demand environment remained firm as the industry prepared for the next-generation accelerator cycle.

## The Runway Visible from Q1

Extrapolating the FY2025 exit run-rate and its seasonal sequential patterns produces a plausible FY2026 revenue range of $1.2 billion to $1.4 billion. This is informed extrapolation, not management guidance; Astera had not, as of May 23, 2026, issued full-year 2026 revenue guidance. But the operating-leverage dynamics are clear enough to model. At $1.2 to $1.4 billion of revenue and a preserved 75% GAAP gross margin, with operating expenses growing at a fraction of the revenue rate, GAAP net income could exceed $400 million for the full year — a result that would place Astera among the most profitable standalone semiconductor companies measured by net income margin at this scale.

| Metric | FY2025 Actual | FY2026 Low Case | FY2026 High Case |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue ($M) | $852.5 | ~$1,200 | ~$1,400 |
| GAAP Gross Margin | 75.7% | ~75% | ~75% |
| Gross Profit ($M) | ~$645 | ~$900 | ~$1,050 |
| GAAP Net Income ($M) | $219.1 | ~$350 | ~$450+ |

*FY2026 figures are informed extrapolation, not company guidance.*

The critical variable is not the revenue trajectory — the Q1 backlog signal suggests continued momentum — but whether Astera's design-in position survives the transition to next-generation accelerator silicon intact.

## The Architecture Transition: Rubin and MI400

The design-in cycle that produced FY2025's 115% revenue growth was predominantly aligned to Nvidia's Hopper and Blackwell accelerator families and the server builds around them. Astera's Aries PCIe and CXL retimers, Taurus smart cable modules, and early Leo CXL memory controller shipments were embedded in the AI server platforms that hyperscalers — Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Google — and OEMs including Supermicro, Dell, and HPE deployed at scale through calendar 2024 and 2025.

The next-generation question is Nvidia Rubin and AMD MI400-series, both expected to reach volume production in the late-2026 to 2027 timeframe. These are not incremental BOM revisions; they are architectural resets. Rubin advances Nvidia's rack-level interconnect architecture. MI400 represents AMD's most aggressive push to close the infrastructure and software gap with Nvidia at scale. Each requires fresh design-in work. Each runs an 18-to-24-month qualification cycle from specification engagement through volume ramp.

Astera had not, as of May 2026, published press releases naming design wins specifically on Rubin or MI400 platforms — the leading indicator that would confirm retention of current connectivity-silicon positioning. The absence is not a negative signal in isolation; design-in relationships are frequently under non-disclosure until customers choose to publicise. The signal to watch for, in the quarters ahead, is precisely those announcements: Astera design-win press releases or server OEM platform launches naming Astera silicon in Rubin and MI400 system configurations.

The scenario split is relatively binary. If Astera retains its Rubin and MI400 design-in positions — which the underlying PCIe Gen6 link physics continue to favour, since every higher-frequency accelerator interconnect increases the technical necessity of active signal conditioning — a 30 to 50% revenue growth trajectory into 2027 is plausible without requiring meaningful Scorpio volume contribution. If Astera loses design-in ground at either next-generation platform, the FY2025 result becomes a structural plateau rather than a step.

The PCIe physics argument is not aspirational framing. At Gen6 link rates, the signal integrity challenge across server board traces and backplane connections is more acute than at Gen5, not less. A retimer at those speeds is a required component, not a discretionary add-on. This is the same structural logic that drove Aries adoption through Hopper and Blackwell, and absent a fundamental architectural departure from PCIe as the universal peripheral interconnect standard, it should persist into Rubin.

## Scorpio: The Optionality Question

The Scorpio product family is where Astera's long-term addressable-market expansion story either begins or stalls. PCIe and CXL fabric switches — Scorpio's territory — connect multiple GPUs through a standards-based fabric, offering an architectural alternative to proprietary interconnects at the rack and pod level. The competitive landscape is formidable: Broadcom holds competing PCIe switching silicon at significantly larger scale, and Nvidia's NVLink and NVSwitch proprietary fabric continues to dominate the highest-performance intra-rack and multi-rack GPU interconnect designs at hyperscale.

The strategic logic for Scorpio is compelling precisely because the competitive landscape outside Nvidia is fractured. Hyperscalers running AMD MI300X and MI400-series clusters, or their own custom silicon programs, carry strong economic and technical incentives to avoid NVLink dependency — and to design AI server fabrics around standards-based PCIe and CXL switching silicon where possible. Scorpio is the Astera product positioned to serve that preference.

The TAM mathematics are straightforward. Astera's current revenue base is dominated by retimers and smart cable modules — high-margin, required components, but with per-unit ASPs measured in tens of dollars per AI server. A fabric switch chip connecting eight, sixteen, or thirty-two GPUs in a pod or rack carries substantially higher per-system ASP, with addressable markets that scale with AI pod count rather than per-server GPU attach rate. Volume design-in at even one or two hyperscale programs by FY2027 could be material relative to the current retimer base.

The risk is that Scorpio remains a niche product. Direct competition with Broadcom's switching silicon and Nvidia's NVSwitch — incumbents with established software ecosystems and multi-year customer relationships — is among the hardest go-to-market environments in AI connectivity. The Enfabrica pattern is instructive: Sutter Hill Ventures (Astera's Series A lead) had also been an Enfabrica investor; Stefan Dyckerhoff's departure from the Enfabrica board in 2025 marked a clear fork in adjacent competitive positioning. Scorpio must prove it can win design-ins at hyperscalers who have already made substantial investments in existing GPU fabric architectures.

The leading indicator for Scorpio will not be a revenue line — not at FY2026 scale — but customer-reference announcements and hyperscaler infrastructure publications naming Scorpio or its PCIe/CXL switching derivatives in production or qualification programs. Until those appear, Scorpio remains an option whose value is real but whose exercise is unconfirmed.

## The Balance Sheet and the M&A Shadow

Astera enters the architecture-transition period with a capital structure unusual for a company at this stage of its public-market life. The $1.19 billion in liquid assets — $167.6 million cash and $1.02 billion in marketable securities — against essentially no funded debt provides a multi-year operational buffer that most semiconductor companies at the $850 million revenue scale do not carry. The $319.3 million in FY2025 operating cash flow suggests the balance sheet is self-reinforcing rather than depleting.

This capital position matters for two reasons. First, it means Astera can sustain its R&D investment through a multi-quarter demand pause should one materialize from hyperscaler capex discipline, without financing pressure. Second, it places the company in a position to execute strategic acquisitions in connectivity-silicon adjacencies without dilutive equity issuance. The appointment of Desmond Lynch as CFO in March 2026 — drawn from Rambus, where semiconductor IP licensing economics dominate the financial profile — suggests the company is thinking carefully about how connectivity IP is monetised as it moves up the stack.

A company carrying $852 million of annual revenue, 75.7% GAAP gross margin, $1.19 billion of liquid assets, and a board whose members have personally navigated the sale of Galileo to Marvell (Manuel Alba), Annapurna Labs to Amazon (Alba again), Habana Labs to Intel (Alba again), Barefoot Networks to Intel (Craig Barratt), and Atheros to Qualcomm (Barratt and Jack Lazar both) is not invisible to acquirers.

Broadcom holds the most direct rationale: Astera's retimer and fabric-switch positioning would strengthen Broadcom's connectivity silicon portfolio for AI infrastructure. The antitrust arithmetic is the obstacle. Marvell — whose original formation included the Galileo acquisition that Alba co-founded and sold — has both the strategic logic and the M&A execution history; the board chair's direct Marvell provenance is not a disclosure, it is a pattern. Nvidia acquiring the leading third-party PCIe/CXL retimer and fabric switch supplier would raise customer-confidence concerns among AMD-platform and hyperscaler-custom-silicon customers that constitute a meaningful portion of Astera's addressable market. Intel — where Barratt assumed the board chairmanship in May 2026, having previously sold Barefoot Networks into the Intel connectivity division — is the most intriguing structural overlap. That overlap is not proof of intent. It is the kind of board-level information density that M&A processes require to move quickly if presented with the right conditions and price.

There is no public signal of any active transaction as of May 23, 2026. What exists instead is the board composition of a company that could execute one.

## The Question This Report Has Built Toward

The structural position Astera Labs assembled between its November 2017 founding and its FY2025 result — 75.7% GAAP gross margin, $852.5 million of revenue, $219 million of GAAP net income, $1.19 billion of liquid capital, three founder-operators in place, and a board assembled with uncommon pattern recognition — is among the more defensible connectivity-semiconductor positions in the current AI infrastructure cycle.

The question that position cannot yet answer is whether it compounds. Rubin and MI400 design-in confirmation is the near-term binary that the FY2026 and FY2027 quarterly prints will resolve. Scorpio volume contribution by FY2027 is the medium-term option whose exercise price is still unknown. The operating-leverage math at $1.2 to $1.4 billion of FY2026 revenue and preserved gross margin is the near-certain consequence of the current setup — but only if the design-in holds.

Astera's founding thesis was that the physics of AI connectivity — rising link speeds, disaggregated memory and accelerator architectures, the signal-integrity requirements of high-radix PCIe fabrics — create a structural role for purpose-built connectivity silicon that neither GPU vendors nor CPU vendors have the business-model incentive to commoditise. FY2025 validated that thesis at $852 million of revenue and 75.7% gross margin. Whether FY2026 and FY2027 confirm it as structure rather than moment is the question the primary record, through May 2026, does not yet answer. The reader has the evidence assembled here. The view from here is theirs to take.
